symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Inspect global-route congestion map hotspots vs. local density reports
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest visual check that rules out pure density overflow versus pin/access or cell-shape issues

first_checks.check: Count and map hard macros, blockages, and keep-out zones near the DRC clusters
first_checks.why_first: Rules out placement legality artifacts that density metrics ignore

first_checks.check: Examine pin density and cell orientation distributions in the failing regions
first_checks.why_first: Discriminates access-limited congestion from pure track shortage

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily inflate cell spacing or add soft blockages only in the hotspot cells and re-run global route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs vanish → local pin/access or orientation packing was the driver
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRCs persist → deeper track or layer-resource shortage

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare congestion after forcing all standard cells to preferred orientation vs. mixed
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Congestion drops sharply with preferred orientation → orientation-induced access conflict
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No change → orientation not causal

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Disable or upsize metal-layer preferred-direction constraints on the congested layers and re-route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs clear → preferred-direction or via-ladder restriction was binding
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Still congested → true capacity shortfall

common_root_causes.cause: High pin-density standard-cell clusters or multi-height cells creating local access conflicts
Hard-macro abutment or channel pinch-offs invisible to average density metrics
Overly aggressive power-grid or via-ladder reservation eating routing tracks
Placement legalization that packed cells into narrow corridors after density check

classic_trap: Treating average or bin density as sufficient and missing local pin-access or orientation hotspots
node_era_note: 7nm-and-below pin-access and multi-patterning constraints make orientation and cut-mask rules far more frequent drivers than at 28nm

first_checks.check: Diff pre-CTS vs post-CTS timing on the same paths and isolate the delta to clock path or data path
first_checks.why_first: Immediately separates pure data-path regression from clock-insertion or skew change

first_checks.check: Extract the common clock-path segments shared by all failing endpoints
first_checks.why_first: Rules out global clock-tree problem versus scattered data-path issues

first_checks.check: Check useful-skew and latency targets versus achieved insertion delays on the failing clocks
first_checks.why_first: Cheap confirmation that CTS met (or missed) the intended balancing

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all failing paths share one clock-gating or buffer cell, replace or upsize only that cell and re-time; else spread the same experiment across unrelated hierarchies
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Shared cell fix clears all → that cell is the bottleneck; spread fix needed → distributed data-path or multiple clock domains
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite pattern excludes the single-cell hypothesis

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Force ideal clocks (zero skew, zero latency) on the failing domains and re-report setup
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Violations disappear → clock-tree insertion/skew is causal
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Violations remain → pure data-path delay increase

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare setup slack when useful-skew is disabled versus enabled on the same CTS result
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Slack recovers only with useful skew → intentional skew was required but not realized
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No difference → useful-skew not the missing ingredient

common_root_causes.cause: CTS inserted extra latency or unbalanced skew that eroded setup margin
Clock-gating or enable logic on the critical path became slower after buffering
Data-path cells detoured or were resized sub-optimally during post-CTS optimization
OCV/AOCV derates applied more pessimistically after real clock tree existed

classic_trap: Blaming data-path cells when the entire slack loss is in the newly inserted clock path
node_era_note: 7nm-and-below AOCV/POCV and multi-corner CTS make clock-path contribution larger and more variable than typical 28nm flows

first_checks.check: Identify whether failing paths are short data paths between closely placed flops on the same clock
first_checks.why_first: Most common and cheapest pattern to confirm

first_checks.check: Measure actual clock skew (including local) on the launch/capture pairs of the violators
first_checks.why_first: Rules out excessive positive skew introduced by CTS

first_checks.check: Check hold derates, clock uncertainty, and any intentional useful skew that became harmful
first_checks.why_first: Quickly isolates constraint versus physical causes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If violators share a common local clock buffer, upsize or rebuffer only that branch; if they are scattered, apply uniform hold buffers on data paths
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Shared-buffer fix clears the cluster → local skew source; scattered data-path buffers needed → pure min-delay shortfall
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite result excludes the clustered-skew hypothesis

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run hold analysis with zero clock uncertainty and minimum derates
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Violations vanish → constraint pessimism was dominant
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Violations remain → real physical min-delay problem

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Force the same insertion delay on launch and capture clocks for the failing pairs and re-report
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Holds clear → skew introduced by CTS is causal
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Holds persist → data-path delay too small independent of skew

common_root_causes.cause: Short data paths between adjacent flops combined with residual positive skew
CTS useful-skew or balancing that favored setup at the expense of hold
Insufficient hold buffers inserted because pre-CTS hold was optimistic
Local clock skew from uneven clock-gate or buffer loading

classic_trap: Over-buffering the data path globally when only a few local clock branches need balancing
node_era_note: 7nm-and-below hold windows shrink and variation increases, making post-CTS hold more frequent and more sensitive to local skew than at 28nm

first_checks.check: Map the failing timing endpoints onto the dynamic or static IR-drop hotspots
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest spatial correlation that confirms or refutes voltage-drop causality

first_checks.check: Compare timing slack with ideal voltage versus the IR-drop-aware voltage map
first_checks.why_first: Quantifies how much of the violation is voltage-induced

first_checks.check: Inspect power-grid density, via counts, and package bump proximity in the hotspot
first_checks.why_first: Rules out obvious grid or packaging weaknesses

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Scale the local supply voltage of only the IR-hotspot instances by the measured drop and re-time; leave other instances ideal
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Violations appear or worsen only on the scaled instances → IR is causal for those paths
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No change → timing failure independent of the observed drop

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add temporary decap or widen power straps only under the failing cluster and re-analyze both IR and timing
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Both IR and timing improve → local grid weakness was the link
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: IR improves but timing does not → timing root is elsewhere

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Vector the highest-activity switching windows that coincide with the timing paths and re-run dynamic IR
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Peak drop aligns with the failing paths → activity-induced dynamic IR
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Peak drop elsewhere → static or unrelated dynamic issue

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient local power-grid density or via stacking under high-activity logic
Simultaneous switching of wide buses or clock gates creating transient droop
Package or bump placement far from the demand hotspot
Overly aggressive power-gating or weak header devices

classic_trap: Assuming any IR hotspot automatically explains the timing path without checking spatial and temporal overlap
node_era_note: 7nm-and-below lower Vdd and higher current density make dynamic IR far more frequent and tighter to timing than typical 28nm designs

symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Plot achieved versus target insertion delay for every sink and identify outlier clusters
first_checks.why_first: Immediate visual separation of global versus local divergence

first_checks.check: Check clock-tree topology reports for missing or blocked buffer sites near the outliers
first_checks.why_first: Rules out placement or blockage obstacles to buffering

first_checks.check: Verify clock-root latency, generated-clock definitions, and any multi-corner target conflicts
first_checks.why_first: Excludes constraint or multi-mode mis-specification

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If outliers share a common upstream buffer or region, force extra buffer levels only on that branch; if outliers are scattered, relax global latency targets
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Branch fix equalizes the cluster → local blockage or loading; global relax needed → overall target infeasible
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite pattern excludes the local-branch hypothesis

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Remove all placement blockages and keep-outs in the outlier regions and re-run CTS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Targets met → physical blockage prevented proper buffering
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Still diverge → capacity, library, or constraint issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run CTS with a single corner/mode versus the full multi-corner set and compare sink latency spread
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Single-corner meets targets, multi-corner diverges → conflicting multi-corner constraints
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Both diverge equally → not a multi-corner conflict

common_root_causes.cause: Placement blockages or macro keep-outs preventing buffer insertion on some branches
Highly unbalanced sink loads or clock-gate clustering
Overly tight or conflicting multi-corner insertion-delay targets
Insufficient buffer library variety or drive-strength steps

classic_trap: Loosening global skew targets when only a few local branches are blocked
node_era_note: 7nm-and-below CTS must also satisfy multi-patterning and via-pillar constraints, increasing divergence frequency versus 28nm

symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Cross-reference the LVS error locations against the corresponding layout and schematic net names
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest way to see whether the mismatch is naming, extraction, or real connectivity

first_checks.check: Inspect the extracted netlist for floating pins, unlabeled metal, or unintended merges near the reported short/open
first_checks.why_first: Rules out pure extraction artifacts

first_checks.check: Check hierarchical versus flat LVS results on the same cell
first_checks.why_first: Discriminates hierarchy boundary problems from true geometry issues

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If the shorted nets belong to different power domains or intended isolated signals, examine the geometry at their closest approach; if they are the same logical net, check for missing via or label
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Different nets touching → real short; same net missing connection → real open
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Geometry clean → extraction or labeling error

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-extract with connectivity-only versus full parasitic extraction and re-run LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Connectivity-only clean, full extraction fails → parasitic or marker issue; both fail → geometric connectivity problem
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite result narrows the cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Promote the failing hierarchical block to flat and re-LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Flat LVS passes → hierarchy or pin-mismatch problem
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Flat still fails → real layout versus schematic discrepancy

common_root_causes.cause: Missing or misaligned vias between metal layers
Unintended metal shorts from over-enclosures or fill
Hierarchical pin or net-name mismatches at block boundaries
Extraction tool missing a device or net because of labeling or soft-check settings

classic_trap: Assuming every LVS short is a real geometry error when many are hierarchical naming or extraction-setting artifacts

symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Compare the reported device parameters (width, length, fingers, multiplier) between layout extraction and schematic
first_checks.why_first: Directly quantifies the size discrepancy

first_checks.check: Inspect the layout for unintended device recognition (e.g., extra poly or diffusion islands)
first_checks.why_first: Rules out extraction creating phantom devices

first_checks.check: Verify schematic source versus the netlist actually used for LVS (including any generated or parameterized cells)
first_checks.why_first: Excludes schematic-side version skew

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If extra devices appear only in extraction, mask or remove the suspicious geometry and re-extract; if sizes differ, force the layout device to schematic dimensions and re-LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Extra-device errors clear after geometry edit → phantom recognition; size errors clear after forced match → real drawn-size mismatch
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Errors persist → deeper rule or tool issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run LVS with device-recognition rules relaxed versus strict and compare extra-device counts
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Extras disappear with relaxed rules → over-aggressive recognition
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Extras remain → true extra geometry

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare LVS using the original schematic versus a schematic regenerated from the layout
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Regenerated matches layout → original schematic was stale or parameterized incorrectly
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Both mismatch → layout itself is wrong

common_root_causes.cause: Layout drawn with incorrect width/length or finger count relative to schematic
Extraction recognizing dummy or fill structures as active devices
Parameterized or PCell expansion mismatch between schematic and layout views
Stale schematic netlist used for LVS after layout ECO

classic_trap: Editing the schematic to match a wrong layout instead of correcting the drawn device geometry

first_checks.check: Map the violating nets and identify the largest metal area ratio relative to the gate or diffusion area
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest confirmation of classic area-ratio antenna

first_checks.check: Check whether diode insertion or metal-jump (layer hopping) rules were enabled in the router
first_checks.why_first: Rules out simple missing-fix-option causes

first_checks.check: Inspect long top-metal routes that land on small gates without intermediate discharge paths
first_checks.why_first: Common physical pattern

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert antenna diodes only on the violating pins and re-check; if still failing, force a metal-layer jump on the same nets
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Diode clears → classic charge accumulation; jump needed → diode insufficient or rule forbids diode
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Neither helps → extraction or rule-deck mismatch

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Break the longest violating metal segment into two by adding a via to a lower layer and back, then re-run antenna check
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Violation clears → pure area-ratio problem solvable by hopping
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Still violates → partial antenna or cumulative multi-layer issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare antenna results with foundry rule deck versus a relaxed internal deck
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Only foundry deck fails → rule interpretation or margin difference
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Both fail equally → real geometric violation

common_root_causes.cause: Long upper-metal routes connected to small gate poly without intermediate vias or diodes
Router antenna-prevention options (diode insertion, hopping) left disabled or constrained too tightly
Cumulative antenna from multiple layers that individually look safe
ECO routes that bypassed the original antenna-aware path

classic_trap: Inserting diodes everywhere when a simple metal hop would have been cheaper and sufficient
node_era_note: 7nm-and-below multi-patterning and thinner gate oxides make antenna rules stricter and diode insertion more constrained than at 28nm

symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Overlay the detailed DRC locations on the global-route congestion and track-usage maps
first_checks.why_first: Confirms whether global route was truly clean or merely averaged away local problems

first_checks.check: Inspect via spacing, end-of-line, and cut-mask rules in the hotspot layers
first_checks.why_first: Many post-global DRCs are via or coloring rule violations invisible to global route

first_checks.check: Check for pin-access or cell-boundary conflicts that global route treated as soft
first_checks.why_first: Common source of localized detailed failures

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If DRCs cluster around vias or pin access, force alternative via structures or pin swaps only in that region; if they follow long routes, relax spacing or widen tracks locally
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Via/pin fix clears → access or via-rule problem; track relax needed → capacity or spacing rule binding
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite result excludes the hypothesized class

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run detailed route with via-pillar or multi-cut vias disabled versus enabled
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs appear only with advanced vias → via-rule or enclosure conflict
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRCs identical → not via-structure related

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Increase local track allocation or reduce adjacent cell density and re-detail-route only the hotspot
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs clear → residual local capacity shortfall that global route missed
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Still fail → pure design-rule (non-capacity) violation

common_root_causes.cause: Via spacing, enclosure, or cut-mask coloring violations invisible to global routing
Pin-access conflicts on multi-height or complex standard cells
Local track shortage after power-grid or blockage finalization
End-of-line or minimum-area metal rules triggered by short jogs

classic_trap: Re-running global route with higher effort when the real problem is detailed via or coloring rules
node_era_note: 7nm-and-below multi-patterning, EUV, and via-pillar rules create far more detailed-only DRCs than classic 28nm double-patterning

symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Examine the overflow or divergence metric progression across global-placement iterations
first_checks.why_first: Shows whether the engine is oscillating, stuck, or steadily worsening

first_checks.check: Map the densest bins against macros, blockages, and fixed-cell regions
first_checks.why_first: Rules out obvious floorplan-induced unroutability

first_checks.check: Compare target density, max utilization, and any density screens versus achieved
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest constraint-versus-result check

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If overflow is concentrated near macros, inflate macro keep-outs or move macros; if overflow is uniform, lower global density target or inflate all cells
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Macro move clears → floorplan pinch; global density reduction needed → pure capacity shortfall
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite pattern excludes the hypothesized class

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run placement with all soft blockages and density screens removed versus fully constrained
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Unconstrained succeeds, constrained fails → blockage or screen over-constraint
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Both fail → fundamental area or cell-count problem

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Replace high-pin-count or large-area cells with smaller equivalents (or remove a non-critical hierarchy) and re-place
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Placement converges → those cells were the packing bottleneck
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Still diverges → broader floorplan or utilization issue

common_root_causes.cause: Floorplan channels or macro placements that create unroutable narrow corridors
Target utilization set higher than the design’s real packing limit given cell mix
Excessive fixed cells, soft blockages, or density screens over-constraining the placer
Pathological cell size mix (many large multi-height cells) preventing legal packing

classic_trap: Raising placement effort or runtime when the floorplan itself is the fundamental bottleneck
node_era_note: 7nm-and-below multi-height cells and stricter pin-access rules make packing failures more frequent than typical 28nm standard-cell libraries
